stem: The guiding principle of independent India's foreign policy, especially under Nehru, was __________.
options: Non-alignment (staying out of the two Cold War blocs and pursuing an independent foreign policy)
solution: The guiding principle of independent India's foreign policy — especially under Jawaharlal NEHRU (who was both PM and Foreign Minister) — was NON-ALIGNMENT: keeping OUT of the two Cold War MILITARY BLOCS (neither the US-led Western camp nor the Soviet-led Eastern camp) and pursuing an INDEPENDENT foreign policy, judging each issue on its merits. This reflected India's determination to protect its hard-won sovereignty and to promote world peace and decolonisation. So India's foreign policy was based on non-alignment. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: The architect of India's foreign policy in the early years, who served as both Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, was __________.
solution: Jawaharlal NEHRU was the chief ARCHITECT of India's foreign policy in the early years. As the first Prime Minister, he ALSO held the portfolio of FOREIGN (External Affairs) Minister, and he personally shaped India's foreign policy — championing NON-ALIGNMENT, Panchsheel, anti-colonialism and anti-racism, world peace, and India's role as a voice of the newly independent nations. His vision defined India's international stance for decades. So the architect of India's foreign policy was Nehru. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The 'Panchsheel' (Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence), enunciated in 1954, were part of an agreement between India and __________.
solution: The PANCHSHEEL — the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence — were formally enunciated in 1954 as part of an AGREEMENT between INDIA and CHINA (specifically, an agreement concerning TIBET). The five principles were: mutual respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty; mutual non-aggression; mutual non-interference in internal affairs; equality and mutual benefit; and peaceful coexistence. They embodied the ideals of India's foreign policy and initially symbolised India–China friendship ('Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai'). So Panchsheel was part of the 1954 India–China agreement. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: India played a leading role in founding the __________, along with countries like Yugoslavia, Egypt, Indonesia, and Ghana.
solution: India played a LEADING role in founding the NON-ALIGNED MOVEMENT (NAM), together with countries like YUGOSLAVIA (Tito), EGYPT (Nasser), INDONESIA (Sukarno), and GHANA (Nkrumah). Nehru was one of the principal architects of NAM, whose first summit was held at Belgrade in 1961. NAM brought together nations that refused to join either Cold War bloc, and India's leadership of it was a cornerstone of its foreign policy and international standing. So India helped found the Non-Aligned Movement. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: India's foreign policy under Nehru also strongly supported __________.
options: Decolonisation (freedom for colonised nations) and opposition to racism/apartheid, and world peace and disarmament
solution: India's foreign policy under Nehru strongly SUPPORTED: DECOLONISATION — championing the FREEDOM of colonised nations in Asia and Africa (India, itself newly free, became a leading voice against colonialism); OPPOSITION to RACISM and APARTHEID (notably condemning apartheid in South Africa); and WORLD PEACE and DISARMAMENT (advocating reduction of Cold War tensions and nuclear weapons). These principled stances gave India significant MORAL standing and leadership among the newly independent and developing nations. So India supported decolonisation, anti-racism, and peace/disarmament. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The India–China relationship deteriorated sharply, culminating in the __________.
options: Sino-Indian War of 1962 (over the disputed border)
solution: The India–China relationship, initially friendly ('Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai'), DETERIORATED sharply over the disputed BORDER and the Tibet issue, culminating in the SINO-INDIAN WAR of 1962. China launched a military attack across the disputed Himalayan boundary; India suffered a serious military DEFEAT. The 1962 war was a major shock and setback for India — damaging its prestige, exposing its military unpreparedness, and dealing a blow to Nehru's policy of friendship with China and to his standing. So the deterioration culminated in the 1962 Sino-Indian War. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: The 1962 war with China was significant for India because it __________.
options: Ended in a military defeat for India, was a blow to Nehru's foreign policy and prestige, and led India to strengthen its defence preparedness
solution: The 1962 war with China was significant because it ended in a MILITARY DEFEAT for India (Indian forces, unprepared and outmatched in the harsh terrain, were pushed back before China declared a unilateral ceasefire). It was a severe BLOW to NEHRU's FOREIGN POLICY (especially his trust in China and Panchsheel) and to his personal PRESTIGE, and it deeply shocked the nation. In its aftermath, India resolved to STRENGTHEN its DEFENCE preparedness (modernising and expanding the armed forces). So the 1962 war was a defeat that damaged Nehru's policy/prestige and spurred defence modernisation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India fought a war with Pakistan in 1965, largely over __________.
solution: India fought a WAR with PAKISTAN in 1965, largely over the disputed region of KASHMIR (Pakistan launched an infiltration/attack aiming to seize Kashmir). The war ended in a stalemate, followed by the TASHKENT Agreement (1966, mediated by the USSR) between India's PM Lal Bahadur Shastri and Pakistan's President Ayub Khan. This was the second India–Pakistan war over Kashmir. So the 1965 war was over Kashmir. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The 1971 war between India and Pakistan led to __________.
options: The creation of Bangladesh (the liberation of East Pakistan), a decisive Indian victory
solution: The 1971 war between India and Pakistan (arising from the crisis in East Pakistan) led to a DECISIVE INDIAN VICTORY and the CREATION of BANGLADESH — the liberation of EAST PAKISTAN, which became the independent nation of Bangladesh. India (under PM Indira Gandhi) intervened militarily in support of the Bengali liberation struggle, and Pakistani forces in the east surrendered. This was a major triumph for India and a transformation of the South Asian map. So the 1971 war created Bangladesh. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: In 1971, in the tense run-up to the war, India signed a Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation with __________.
solution: In August 1971, in the tense build-up to the war (with Pakistan being backed by the USA and China), India signed a 20-year Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation with the SOVIET UNION (USSR). This treaty provided India with important diplomatic and potential security BACKING during the 1971 crisis and war, helping to deter US/Chinese intervention on Pakistan's behalf. It marked a tilt toward the USSR (though India maintained it was consistent with its interests). So the 1971 treaty was with the USSR. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: India conducted its first nuclear test in __________.
solution: India conducted its FIRST NUCLEAR TEST in 1974 — a nuclear device detonated at POKHRAN (in Rajasthan), described by India as a 'PEACEFUL NUCLEAR EXPLOSION' (codenamed 'Smiling Buddha'). This demonstrated India's nuclear capability. India later conducted a further series of nuclear tests in 1998 (Pokhran-II), after which it declared itself a nuclear-weapon state. So India's first nuclear test was in 1974. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: India has refused to sign the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) because it considers the treaty __________.
options: Discriminatory (it divides the world into nuclear 'haves' and 'have-nots', legitimising the arsenals of a few while denying others)
solution: India has REFUSED to sign the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) because it considers the treaty DISCRIMINATORY. India argues that the NPT unfairly DIVIDES the world into nuclear 'HAVES' (the five recognised nuclear-weapon states, whose arsenals it legitimises) and 'HAVE-NOTS' (all other countries, who are permanently barred from acquiring nuclear weapons) — a discriminatory, unequal arrangement that entrenches the monopoly of a few powers while denying the same right to others. India has called instead for universal, non-discriminatory disarmament. So India rejects the NPT as discriminatory. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The 1962 war was a turning point in India's foreign and defence policy. Reason (R): The defeat by China shattered illusions about Panchsheel-based friendship and prompted India to modernise its military and reassess its security. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the 1962 war was a TURNING POINT in India's foreign and defence policy. And the reason is (R) that the DEFEAT by CHINA SHATTERED the illusions about the PANCHSHEEL-based friendship ('Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai') and India's idealistic assumptions, and PROMPTED India to seriously MODERNISE and expand its MILITARY and to REASSESS its security and strategic outlook (paying more attention to hard power and defence). This rude awakening and its consequences directly made 1962 a turning point (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): India signed a friendship treaty with the USSR in 1971. Reason (R): Facing a looming war with Pakistan (which was backed by the USA and China), India sought Soviet support to protect its interests. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India signed a Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation with the USSR in 1971. And the reason is (R) that India was facing a LOOMING WAR with PAKISTAN over the East Pakistan/Bangladesh crisis, and Pakistan was BACKED by the USA and CHINA — so India SOUGHT SOVIET SUPPORT (diplomatic and strategic backing, and a counter to possible US/Chinese pressure) to PROTECT its INTERESTS during the crisis. This strategic need for a counterweight and support directly explains why India signed the treaty with the USSR at that moment (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: India's foreign policy after Nehru showed both continuity and change. Which of the following reflects continuity?
options: The broad commitment to non-alignment, an independent foreign policy, and pursuit of national interest remained, even as India became more pragmatic and security-conscious
India abandoned all its earlier principles
India stopped having a foreign policy
solution: India's foreign policy after Nehru showed both CONTINUITY and change. The CONTINUITY lay in the broad commitment to NON-ALIGNMENT, an INDEPENDENT FOREIGN POLICY, and the pursuit of India's NATIONAL INTEREST and sovereignty — these core principles persisted under later leaders. The CHANGE was that India became more PRAGMATIC, REALISTIC, and SECURITY-CONSCIOUS (especially after the 1962 shock) — placing greater emphasis on military strength, strategic partnerships (like the 1971 Soviet treaty), and hard national interest, tempering the earlier idealism. So the continuity was the persistence of non-alignment and independent foreign policy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The slogan 'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai' expressed the __________.
options: Early friendship and brotherhood between India and China (before the 1962 war)
solution: The slogan 'HINDI-CHINI BHAI-BHAI' ('Indians and Chinese are brothers') expressed the EARLY FRIENDSHIP and sense of BROTHERHOOD between INDIA and CHINA in the 1950s — a period of warm relations symbolised by Panchsheel and India's championing of China internationally. This goodwill, however, was shattered by the border dispute and the 1962 WAR. The slogan is remembered as an emblem of the hopeful (and ultimately disappointed) early India–China relationship. So it expressed early India–China friendship. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Tashkent Agreement (1966) was signed after the 1965 war between India and Pakistan, and was mediated by __________.
solution: The TASHKENT AGREEMENT (1966) was signed after the 1965 India–Pakistan war (over Kashmir) between India's PM Lal Bahadur SHASTRI and Pakistan's President Ayub Khan. It was MEDIATED by the SOVIET UNION (USSR), at Tashkent (in Soviet Central Asia). Under it, the two sides agreed to withdraw to pre-war positions and restore normal relations. (Shastri died in Tashkent shortly after signing.) So the Tashkent Agreement was mediated by the USSR. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The Shimla Agreement (1972) between India and Pakistan, signed after the 1971 war, committed the two countries to __________.
options: Resolving their disputes (including Kashmir) bilaterally and peacefully, and respecting the Line of Control
Handing Kashmir to a third country
solution: The SHIMLA AGREEMENT (1972), signed after the 1971 war between India's PM Indira Gandhi and Pakistan's President Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, committed the two countries to RESOLVING their DISPUTES (including KASHMIR) BILATERALLY and PEACEFULLY (without third-party intervention), and to RESPECTING the LINE of CONTROL (the ceasefire line in Kashmir). It aimed to establish a framework for peaceful relations after the war. So the Shimla Agreement committed them to bilateral, peaceful dispute-resolution and respecting the LoC. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: India's foreign policy sought to protect its national interest while also __________, reflecting a blend of realism and idealism.
options: Upholding moral principles and values (peace, anti-colonialism, non-alignment) on the world stage
solution: India's foreign policy sought to PROTECT its NATIONAL INTEREST (security, sovereignty, development) WHILE ALSO UPHOLDING MORAL PRINCIPLES and VALUES on the world stage — such as PEACE, ANTI-COLONIALISM and anti-racism, disarmament, and NON-ALIGNMENT. This distinctive BLEND of REALISM (pursuing hard interests) and IDEALISM (championing ethical principles and a better world order) characterised India's approach, especially under Nehru. India tried to be both a responsible defender of its own interests and a principled voice for justice and peace globally. So it blended national interest with moral principles. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Non-Aligned Movement gave India and other newly independent countries the ability to __________.
options: Pursue independent policies, avoid entanglement in superpower conflicts, and have a collective voice for the developing world
solution: The NON-ALIGNED MOVEMENT gave India and other newly independent countries important capabilities: to PURSUE INDEPENDENT policies (deciding issues on their own judgement rather than a bloc's dictates); to AVOID ENTANGLEMENT in the SUPERPOWERS' CONFLICTS and wars; and to have a COLLECTIVE VOICE and greater bargaining power for the DEVELOPING WORLD on global issues (decolonisation, disarmament, economic justice). For India, leadership of NAM enhanced its independence, security, and international influence. So NAM enabled independent policies, avoidance of superpower conflicts, and a collective developing-world voice. So option 1 is correct.

stem: After the 1962 war, India's relations with the two superpowers involved __________.
options: Receiving military and other assistance from both the USA and the USSR at various times, while maintaining non-alignment
Cutting off all relations with both
solution: After the 1962 war (which exposed India's military weakness), India's relations with the two SUPERPOWERS involved RECEIVING MILITARY and other ASSISTANCE from BOTH the USA and the USSR at various times (both were willing to help India, partly to win its favour and counter China/each other), WHILE India MAINTAINED its policy of NON-ALIGNMENT (not formally joining either bloc). Over time, however, India developed closer ties with the USSR (especially by 1971). This balancing — drawing support from both sides without full alignment — reflected non-alignment in practice. So India received aid from both superpowers while staying non-aligned. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): India refused to sign the NPT and the CTBT. Reason (R): India objected to their discriminatory nature and insisted on retaining its strategic autonomy and the option to develop its nuclear deterrent. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India REFUSED to sign the NPT (and the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, CTBT). And the reason is (R) that India OBJECTED to their DISCRIMINATORY nature (dividing the world into nuclear haves and have-nots, or freezing the status quo in favour of the existing nuclear powers) and INSISTED on retaining its STRATEGIC AUTONOMY and the OPTION to develop its own nuclear DETERRENT for its security. This principled objection to discrimination, combined with security-driven insistence on autonomy, directly explains India's refusal to sign (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The evolution of India's foreign policy shows that a country's external relations are shaped by __________.
options: Both its ideals/values and its practical national interests and security concerns, adapting to changing circumstances
Only the wishes of foreign powers
solution: The evolution of India's foreign policy shows that a country's EXTERNAL RELATIONS are shaped by BOTH its IDEALS/VALUES (like India's commitment to peace, non-alignment, and anti-colonialism) AND its practical NATIONAL INTERESTS and SECURITY concerns (defence, sovereignty, economic needs) — and that policy ADAPTS to CHANGING CIRCUMSTANCES (such as wars, shifting alliances, and the end of the Cold War). India's journey from Nehruvian idealism to a more pragmatic, security-conscious stance (after 1962 and beyond) illustrates this interplay of principle and interest in a changing world. So foreign policy is shaped by both ideals and interests, adapting over time. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The India–China border dispute centres on differing claims along the boundary, including areas in __________.
options: The eastern sector (Arunachal Pradesh / NEFA) and the western sector (Aksai Chin)
solution: The India–CHINA BORDER DISPUTE centres on differing claims along the long Himalayan boundary, involving two main areas: the EASTERN SECTOR — around present-day ARUNACHAL PRADESH (then the North-East Frontier Agency, NEFA), which China claims; and the WESTERN SECTOR — AKSAI CHIN (a high plateau adjoining Ladakh), which India claims but China controls. Disagreement over these territories (and the alignment of the boundary) was the core of the conflict that led to the 1962 war and remains unresolved. So the disputed areas are in the eastern sector (Arunachal/NEFA) and western sector (Aksai Chin). This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: India's grant of asylum to the Dalai Lama in 1959 was a factor that __________.
options: Strained India–China relations (China resented India sheltering the Tibetan spiritual leader who had fled after an uprising in Tibet)
solution: India's grant of ASYLUM to the DALAI LAMA in 1959 (after he fled Tibet following a failed uprising against Chinese control) was a factor that STRAINED India–CHINA relations. CHINA deeply RESENTED India sheltering the Tibetan spiritual leader and his followers, viewing it as interference and encouragement of Tibetan separatism. Along with the border dispute, the Tibet/Dalai Lama issue contributed to the worsening of relations that culminated in the 1962 war. So the asylum to the Dalai Lama strained India–China relations. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: In summary, India's external relations in this period reflect __________.
options: The effort to chart an independent, principled, yet interest-based course through the Cold War — championing non-alignment and peace while defending its security and interests amid regional conflicts and great-power rivalry
A total absence of foreign relations
solution: In summary, India's external relations in this period reflect its EFFORT to CHART an INDEPENDENT, PRINCIPLED, yet INTEREST-BASED COURSE through the Cold War world. India CHAMPIONED NON-ALIGNMENT, world PEACE, decolonisation, and Panchsheel (leading the Non-Aligned Movement and giving voice to the developing world), WHILE also DEFENDING its own SECURITY and national INTERESTS — as it had to amid REGIONAL CONFLICTS (the wars with China in 1962 and Pakistan in 1965 and 1971) and GREAT-POWER RIVALRY (balancing between and drawing support from the superpowers, and pursuing nuclear capability). This blend of idealism and pragmatism, independence and adaptation, defines India's foreign-policy journey in these decades. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Prime Minister who led India during the 1965 war with Pakistan and gave the slogan 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' was __________.
solution: Lal Bahadur SHASTRI was the Prime Minister who led India during the 1965 WAR with Pakistan. He is famous for the inspiring slogan 'JAI JAWAN, JAI KISAN' ('Hail the soldier, Hail the farmer'), honouring the soldiers defending the country and the farmers feeding it — apt at a time of both war and food shortages. Shastri (Nehru's successor) died at Tashkent in January 1966 shortly after signing the Tashkent Agreement. So the PM during the 1965 war was Lal Bahadur Shastri. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The Prime Minister who led India during the 1971 war (creation of Bangladesh) and the 1974 nuclear test was __________.
solution: Indira GANDHI was the Prime Minister who led India during the 1971 WAR with Pakistan that resulted in the creation of BANGLADESH (a major triumph that greatly enhanced her stature), and also during India's FIRST NUCLEAR TEST in 1974 (Pokhran-I). Her tenure marked a more assertive, security-conscious phase of Indian foreign policy. So the PM during the 1971 war and the 1974 nuclear test was Indira Gandhi. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The war of 1962 exposed weaknesses in India's __________, prompting reforms.
options: Military preparedness and intelligence (leading to modernisation and expansion of the armed forces)
solution: The war of 1962 EXPOSED serious WEAKNESSES in India's MILITARY PREPAREDNESS, equipment, planning, and INTELLIGENCE — the armed forces had been under-resourced and were caught unprepared for the Chinese attack in the difficult Himalayan terrain. This shock PROMPTED significant REFORMS: India undertook to MODERNISE and EXPAND its ARMED FORCES, improve defence planning and intelligence, and boost defence spending and indigenous defence production. So the 1962 war exposed weaknesses in military preparedness/intelligence, prompting reforms. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's relations with the USA in the early decades were often __________.
options: Cool or uneasy at times (due to India's non-alignment, US ties with Pakistan, and Cold War differences), though the two remained the world's two large democracies
solution: India's relations with the USA in the early decades were often COOL or UNEASY at times. This was due to several factors: India's policy of NON-ALIGNMENT (which the USA, seeking Cold War allies, sometimes viewed with suspicion or disapproval); the USA's close military TIES with PAKISTAN (India's rival); and broader COLD WAR DIFFERENCES (India's tilt toward the USSR by 1971, and disagreements over various issues). Nonetheless, the two remained the world's two LARGE DEMOCRACIES and cooperated in some areas (e.g., food aid, and post-1962 assistance). So India–US relations were often cool/uneasy in this period. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly lists the wars India fought in this period and their outcomes?
solution: The correct listing of India's wars in this period and their outcomes is: 1962 (with CHINA) — a DEFEAT for India (over the border dispute); 1965 (with PAKISTAN, over Kashmir) — essentially a STALEMATE, followed by the Tashkent Agreement (1966); and 1971 (with PAKISTAN, over the Bangladesh crisis) — a decisive Indian VICTORY, resulting in the creation of BANGLADESH. Knowing these three wars, their opponents, and their outcomes is prelims-critical. So option 1 correctly lists them. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The China factor pushed India and __________ closer together over the following decades.
options: The Soviet Union (and later, in a different era, also the USA), as India sought partners to balance China
The Warsaw Pact as a member
solution: The CHINA FACTOR (the rivalry and security threat from China, especially after 1962) pushed India and the SOVIET UNION closer together over the following decades — the USSR (itself at odds with China after the Sino-Soviet split) became India's key strategic partner and arms supplier (culminating in the 1971 treaty). In a LATER era (after the Cold War, and with China's continued rise), the same balancing logic drew India and the USA closer as well. Thus the need to BALANCE China shaped India's search for major-power partners. So the China factor pushed India toward the USSR (and later the USA). So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): India championed the cause of Asian and African nations. Reason (R): As a newly independent country that had fought colonialism, India felt solidarity with other colonised/newly free peoples and sought to lead the developing world. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India CHAMPIONED the cause of ASIAN and AFRICAN nations. And the reason is (R) that, as a NEWLY INDEPENDENT country that had itself FOUGHT COLONIALISM, India felt deep SOLIDARITY with other colonised and newly free peoples, supported their DECOLONISATION and development, and sought to LEAD the DEVELOPING WORLD (through forums like the Asian Relations Conference, Bandung, and NAM). This shared anti-colonial identity and leadership aspiration directly explain India's championing of Afro-Asian causes (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: V.K. Krishna Menon, a prominent figure in India's early diplomacy, was known as __________.
options: A close associate of Nehru and a forceful diplomat/Defence Minister (whose tenure was, however, tarnished by the 1962 debacle)
A leader of the Muslim League
solution: V.K. Krishna MENON was a prominent figure in India's early diplomacy — a close ASSOCIATE of NEHRU, a forceful and articulate DIPLOMAT (representing India at the UN, known for his long, combative speeches) and India's DEFENCE MINISTER. However, his tenure as Defence Minister was TARNISHED by the 1962 DEBACLE against China (for which he was blamed and had to resign). He remains a notable, if controversial, figure of the Nehru era's foreign and defence policy. So Krishna Menon was Nehru's associate and Defence Minister, associated with the 1962 setback. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The liberation of Goa in 1961 refers to __________.
options: India taking over Goa (and Daman and Diu) from Portuguese colonial rule through military action
solution: The LIBERATION of GOA in 1961 refers to India TAKING OVER Goa (along with Daman and Diu) from PORTUGUESE COLONIAL RULE through a MILITARY ACTION ('Operation Vijay'). Portugal had refused to give up its colonial possessions in India even after 1947, so India ultimately used force to end Portuguese rule and integrate these territories into the Indian Union. This completed the decolonisation of the subcontinent. So the liberation of Goa was India ending Portuguese colonial rule there. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The overall character of India's foreign policy can be summed up as __________.
options: Independent and non-aligned, principled yet pragmatic, aimed at protecting sovereignty and security while promoting peace and a fairer world order
solution: The overall CHARACTER of India's foreign policy can be summed up as INDEPENDENT and NON-ALIGNED, PRINCIPLED yet PRAGMATIC. It aimed at PROTECTING India's SOVEREIGNTY and SECURITY (defending its interests, and adapting to threats like the China challenge), WHILE also PROMOTING PEACE, disarmament, decolonisation, and a FAIRER WORLD ORDER (championing the developing world). This combination — safeguarding national interest without abandoning its ideals, and keeping its independence while engaging actively with the world — defines India's distinctive foreign-policy identity. So it was independent, non-aligned, principled yet pragmatic. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's second round of nuclear tests, after which it openly declared itself a nuclear-weapon state, took place in __________.
solution: India's SECOND round of nuclear tests — Pokhran-II — took place in 1998, after which India OPENLY DECLARED itself a NUCLEAR-WEAPON state. (Pakistan conducted its own tests soon after.) This built on India's first test of 1974 and marked India's overt nuclearisation. (Note: this event is slightly beyond the core Nehru-era timeframe but is important context for India's nuclear policy.) So India's second nuclear tests were in 1998. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The chapter shows that a small country's or new nation's foreign policy is important because __________.
options: It affects the nation's security, development, prestige, and relationships, and shapes its place and role in the world
It has no effect on the country
Only big countries have foreign policy
solution: The chapter shows that FOREIGN POLICY is important for any nation — including a newly independent country like India — because it directly AFFECTS the nation's SECURITY (defending against threats), its DEVELOPMENT (trade, aid, technology, and a peaceful environment for growth), its PRESTIGE and influence, and its RELATIONSHIPS with other states, and it SHAPES the country's PLACE and ROLE in the WORLD. India's careful crafting of its foreign policy (non-alignment, leadership of NAM, managing its neighbours and the superpowers) was thus vital to securing its interests and standing. So foreign policy matters because it shapes a nation's security, development, and world role. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The 1971 war greatly enhanced India's stature in South Asia. Reason (R): India's decisive victory and the creation of Bangladesh established it as the pre-eminent power in the region. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the 1971 war greatly ENHANCED India's STATURE in South Asia. And the reason is (R) that India's DECISIVE MILITARY VICTORY over Pakistan and the CREATION of BANGLADESH (dismembering Pakistan and demonstrating India's military and diplomatic strength) ESTABLISHED India as the clearly PRE-EMINENT POWER in the region. This dramatic display of power and its regional consequences directly explain the boost to India's stature (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The evolution from Nehru's idealism to a more realist foreign policy was driven especially by __________.
options: The shock of the 1962 defeat and subsequent security challenges, which underscored the need for military strength and hard-headed strategy
A sudden increase in India's wealth
The end of the freedom struggle
solution: The EVOLUTION from Nehru's IDEALISM toward a more REALIST foreign policy was driven ESPECIALLY by the SHOCK of the 1962 DEFEAT by China and the SUBSEQUENT SECURITY CHALLENGES (the wars with Pakistan, the China–Pakistan nexus, and Cold War pressures). These experiences painfully UNDERSCORED the need for MILITARY STRENGTH, defence preparedness, strategic alliances (like the 1971 Soviet treaty), and a more HARD-HEADED, interest-based STRATEGY — tempering the earlier reliance on moral principles and goodwill. So the shift to realism was driven mainly by the 1962 defeat and later security challenges. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's approach of non-alignment is best described as __________.
options: A positive, active strategy of independence and engagement (not passive neutrality or isolation)
solution: India's NON-ALIGNMENT is best described as a POSITIVE, ACTIVE STRATEGY of INDEPENDENCE and ENGAGEMENT — NOT passive neutrality or isolation. Non-aligned India engaged VIGOROUSLY in world affairs: taking clear positions on issues (decolonisation, apartheid, disarmament, specific conflicts), mediating and reducing Cold War tensions, leading the Non-Aligned Movement, and maintaining relations with all countries — all while refusing to subordinate its policy to either bloc. Thus non-alignment was an assertive, principled, and engaged foreign policy, not withdrawal from the world. So it was a positive, active strategy of independence and engagement. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'Sino-Soviet split' (the falling out between China and the USSR) was significant for India because __________.
options: It made the USSR more willing to support India (against their common rival, China), strengthening India–USSR ties
It united China and the USSR against India
It had no relevance to India
solution: The 'SINO-SOVIET SPLIT' — the ideological and geopolitical FALLING OUT between COMMUNIST CHINA and the USSR from the late 1950s/1960s — was significant for India because it made the SOVIET UNION MORE WILLING to SUPPORT India: since China had become a common RIVAL/adversary of both the USSR and India (especially after 1962), the USSR saw value in backing India as a counterweight to China. This convergence STRENGTHENED India–USSR TIES (culminating in the 1971 treaty and Soviet arms and diplomatic support). So the Sino-Soviet split helped bring India and the USSR closer. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall significance of studying India's external relations in this period is that it helps us understand __________.
options: The foundations of India's foreign policy, its key relationships and conflicts, and how idealism and realism combined to shape India's role in the world — providing context for its foreign policy today
solution: The overall SIGNIFICANCE of studying India's external relations in this period is that it helps us understand: the FOUNDATIONS of India's FOREIGN POLICY (non-alignment, Panchsheel, leadership of NAM, and the pursuit of independence and peace); its KEY RELATIONSHIPS and CONFLICTS (with China, Pakistan, and the superpowers, including the 1962, 1965, and 1971 wars); and HOW IDEALISM and REALISM COMBINED to shape India's ROLE in the WORLD. This historical understanding provides essential CONTEXT for interpreting India's foreign policy and international position TODAY. So studying it illuminates the foundations, relationships, and evolution of India's foreign policy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a leader with a foreign-policy milestone?
options: Nehru — non-alignment and Panchsheel; Shastri — the 1965 war and Tashkent; Indira Gandhi — the 1971 war, Bangladesh, and the 1974 nuclear test
Nehru — the 1971 war; Shastri — non-alignment; Indira Gandhi — Panchsheel
All milestones belong to one leader
None of these leaders had any role
solution: The correct pairing is: Jawaharlal NEHRU — associated with NON-ALIGNMENT, PANCHSHEEL, the founding of NAM, and the 1962 war; Lal Bahadur SHASTRI — the 1965 WAR with Pakistan and the TASHKENT Agreement; and Indira GANDHI — the 1971 WAR and the creation of BANGLADESH, and the 1974 NUCLEAR TEST. Matching each leader to their foreign-policy milestones is prelims-relevant. So option 1 gives the correct pairing. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The idea behind Panchsheel (peaceful coexistence) was that __________.
options: Countries with different political systems could coexist peacefully by respecting each other's sovereignty and not interfering in each other's affairs
Countries must all have the same government
War is the only way to relate to neighbours
solution: The idea behind PANCHSHEEL (peaceful coexistence) was that countries with DIFFERENT political and ideological SYSTEMS (e.g., communist and non-communist, or of varying kinds) could nonetheless COEXIST PEACEFULLY by RESPECTING each other's SOVEREIGNTY and territorial integrity, refraining from AGGRESSION, and NOT INTERFERING in each other's internal affairs — while dealing with one another on the basis of equality and mutual benefit. It offered a framework for peaceful international relations across ideological divides, reflecting India's hopes for a cooperative world order. So Panchsheel meant peaceful coexistence through mutual respect and non-interference. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): India's foreign policy sometimes disappointed those who expected it to always match its idealistic rhetoric. Reason (R): In practice, India, like all states, had to make compromises and hard choices to protect its national interest and security. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India's foreign policy sometimes DISAPPOINTED those who expected it to ALWAYS MATCH its IDEALISTIC RHETORIC (of peace, non-alignment, and principle). And the reason is (R) that, in PRACTICE, India — like ALL states — had to make COMPROMISES and HARD CHOICES to PROTECT its NATIONAL INTEREST and SECURITY (for example, the use of force in Goa and the 1971 war, the tilt toward the USSR, and the pursuit of nuclear weapons). Because the demands of interest and security sometimes required actions that departed from pure idealism, the gap between rhetoric and practice arose (A). So R correctly explains A. This is a realistic assessment of any nation's foreign policy.

stem: In conclusion, India's external relations reflect a nation __________.
options: Seeking to secure its independence, interests, and security while contributing to a more peaceful and just world — balancing principle and pragmatism through a changing international environment
solution: In conclusion, India's external relations reflect a NATION seeking to SECURE its INDEPENDENCE, INTERESTS, and SECURITY, WHILE also CONTRIBUTING to a more PEACEFUL and JUST WORLD (through non-alignment, anti-colonialism, disarmament advocacy, and leadership of the developing world) — BALANCING PRINCIPLE and PRAGMATISM as it navigated a CHANGING and often dangerous INTERNATIONAL ENVIRONMENT (the Cold War, regional conflicts, and great-power rivalries). India's foreign-policy journey embodies this ongoing effort to reconcile its values with its interests. So India sought its independence and interests while contributing to a better world, balancing principle and pragmatism. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter's discussion of India's external relations is closely linked to the domestic story because __________.
options: Foreign-policy events (like wars and their outcomes) had major effects on Indian domestic politics, leadership, and public mood, and vice versa
Foreign and domestic affairs are completely unrelated
solution: The chapter's discussion of India's EXTERNAL relations is closely LINKED to the DOMESTIC story because FOREIGN-POLICY events had major EFFECTS on Indian domestic POLITICS, LEADERSHIP, and PUBLIC MOOD — and vice versa. For example, the 1962 DEFEAT by China shook Nehru's standing and the nation's confidence; the 1965 and 1971 WARS shaped the fortunes and stature of leaders like Shastri and Indira Gandhi (the 1971 victory greatly boosting Indira Gandhi domestically); and domestic politics in turn influenced foreign-policy choices. Thus the external and internal stories are deeply intertwined. So foreign-policy events and domestic politics strongly affected each other. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Bandung Conference (1955), which India helped organise, was significant because it __________.
options: Brought together Asian and African nations to promote solidarity, decolonisation, and cooperation, and laid the groundwork for the Non-Aligned Movement
Was a meeting of European colonial powers
solution: The BANDUNG CONFERENCE (the Asian-African Conference of 1955, held in Bandung, Indonesia), which India (Nehru) helped organise and lead, was significant because it BROUGHT TOGETHER the ASIAN and AFRICAN nations to promote AFRO-ASIAN SOLIDARITY, support DECOLONISATION and national liberation, oppose colonialism and racism, and foster COOPERATION and peaceful coexistence among the newly independent countries. It marked a milestone in the assertion of the developing world and LAID the GROUNDWORK for the NON-ALIGNED MOVEMENT (founded in 1961). India's prominent role at Bandung enhanced its leadership of the Afro-Asian bloc. So Bandung promoted Afro-Asian solidarity and paved the way for NAM. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'India's External Relations' is that:
options: India had no foreign policy of its own

Independent India, especially under Nehru, developed a distinctive foreign policy based on NON-ALIGNMENT (staying out of the Cold War blocs while pursuing an independent path), the promotion of world peace, decolonisation, anti-racism, and Panchsheel — with India playing a leading role in the Non-Aligned Movement — while also facing hard challenges from its neighbourhood (the 1962 war with China, and wars with Pakistan in 1965 and 1971 that created Bangladesh) that made it more security-conscious and pragmatic; India also pursued nuclear capability (tests in 1974) and an independent stance (refusing the 'discriminatory' NPT), balancing idealism with national interest as it navigated the Cold War world
India simply followed the USA in everything
India was isolated from the world
solution: The chapter's overall message is that independent India — especially under Jawaharlal NEHRU (its architect and long-serving PM/Foreign Minister) — developed a DISTINCTIVE and INDEPENDENT FOREIGN POLICY centred on NON-ALIGNMENT: staying OUT of the two Cold War MILITARY BLOCS while pursuing its own path and judging issues on their merits. India's foreign policy also promoted WORLD PEACE and DISARMAMENT, DECOLONISATION (freedom for colonised peoples), ANTI-RACISM (opposing apartheid), and the ideals of PANCHSHEEL (the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, enunciated with China in 1954) — and India played a LEADING role in founding and guiding the NON-ALIGNED MOVEMENT (with Tito, Nasser, Sukarno, and Nkrumah). At the same time, India faced HARD CHALLENGES from its NEIGHBOURHOOD that tested and reshaped its policy: the traumatic 1962 WAR with CHINA (a military defeat that shattered illusions and spurred defence modernisation), and the WARS with PAKISTAN in 1965 (over Kashmir) and 1971 (which led to the creation of BANGLADESH, with India signing a friendship treaty with the USSR amid US/Chinese backing of Pakistan). These experiences made India more SECURITY-CONSCIOUS and PRAGMATIC. India also pursued NUCLEAR capability (its first test in 1974) and maintained an INDEPENDENT stance (refusing to sign the NPT, which it deemed DISCRIMINATORY). Throughout, India sought to BALANCE its founding IDEALISM (peace, non-alignment, anti-colonialism) with the demands of NATIONAL INTEREST and security as it navigated the dangerous Cold War world. So the overall message is option 2.
